questions.q: Why does capacity planning use peak concurrent load rather than average load?
options: Average load is always higher than peak load
A fleet sized only for average load will fall over during every peak, which is exactly when capacity matters most
Peak load is always identical to average load in practice
Average load cannot be measured for inference services
questions.explain: If capacity is sized for the average, the fleet has no margin for the periods of highest demand — precisely when falling short causes the most visible problems.

questions.q: Why should the 'per-replica capacity' figure come from real benchmarks rather than a vendor's marketing throughput number?
options: Vendor numbers are always deliberately false
Marketing throughput is usually measured without a latency constraint, so it doesn't reflect how much load a replica can take while still meeting your actual SLO
Vendor numbers only apply to CPUs, never GPUs
Benchmarks are only useful for marketing purposes, not capacity planning
questions.explain: A replica can often process more tokens/sec if you let latency blow up, which is what unconstrained marketing throughput numbers typically measure. Real capacity planning needs the throughput achievable while still meeting the SLO.

questions.q: What two distinct needs does a 'headroom factor' typically cover?
options: Marketing budget and sales headcount
Spike headroom (demand beyond forecast) and failover headroom (capacity to absorb a node or zone failure)
Only the cost of electricity for the GPUs
The time it takes to train a new model
questions.explain: Headroom buys time for autoscaling to react to unplanned spikes, and separately ensures that if some capacity fails (a node, a zone), the remaining fleet can still hold the SLO.

questions.q: In the capacity-planning example, what would happen to the required replica count if peak RPS increased from 450 to 600 while per-replica capacity and headroom stayed the same?
options: The replica count would decrease
The replica count would increase, since more peak load divided by the same per-replica capacity requires more replicas
The replica count would stay exactly the same
The formula does not depend on peak RPS at all
questions.explain: Replicas needed scales directly with peak RPS divided by proven per-replica capacity — a higher peak load requires proportionally more replicas, all else equal.

questions.q: Why is spot/preemptible capacity a poor fit for the SLO-critical baseline, even though it's the cheapest option?
options: Spot capacity is always slower than reserved capacity
Spot capacity can be reclaimed by the provider with little notice, making it unsuitable for the steady capacity an SLO depends on
Spot capacity cannot run GPU workloads at all
Spot capacity is more expensive than reserved capacity
questions.explain: Because spot/preemptible instances can be reclaimed with little warning, they fit burst capacity that can tolerate interruption, not the steady baseline that must reliably hold the committed SLO.
